1.title: Transparent and Explainable Models
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: Transparent and Explainable Models. This module covers task statement four point two, and closes Domain four. You will learn the difference between transparent, explainable and opaque models, the tools that document and explain them, the trade-offs involved, and the principles of human-centered design. The exam asks you to recognize why these qualities matter, and to name the right tool or principle.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Tell transparent and explainable models from those that are not. Name the tools: SageMaker Model Cards, A I Service Cards and Bedrock Model Evaluation. Weigh open source models, data and licensing. Describe the trade-offs between safety, transparency, interpretability and performance. And apply human-centered design for explainable A I.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Must Explain Itself
1.text: At Cedar and Salt Travel, a guest is refused a loyalty reward by an A I model, and asks why. Regulators and auditors ask what the model is for, and how it was tested. The team can choose between a simple model and a more accurate, complex one. Your job is to choose models, documents and designs that let people understand.

1.title: Transparent, Explainable and Opaque Models
1.text: Three kinds of model matter here. A transparent model is one where you can know how it was built: the data, the design and the limits are documented and open to review. An explainable model can tell you why it gave an output, for example which features mattered, even if the model is complex. A model that is neither is opaque, or a black box: little is disclosed, and no reasons can be given. A W S describes explainability as understanding and evaluating system outputs, and transparency as letting people make informed choices. Exam tip: transparent is about how it was built, and explainable is about why it answered.

1.title: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards
1.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards document a model's critical details in one place, for governance and reporting. They record the intended uses, including what the model is for and what it is not for, plus the assumptions made. They hold a risk rating of unknown, low, medium or high. They also capture training details and metrics, evaluation results, and caveats and recommendations. Edits create new versions, which gives an immutable record, and you can export a card as a P D F. They support audits and link the model to business goals. Exam tip: one document for a model's purpose, risk, training and evaluation means SageMaker Model Cards.

1.title: AI Service Cards and Other Transparency Tools
1.text: Several tools support transparency. A W S A I Service Cards give a single place to find the intended use cases, limitations, responsible A I design choices and performance best practices of A W S A I services. Amazon SageMaker Clarify explains which input features drove a prediction. Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation gives evidence of quality, toxicity, robustness and faithfulness. And Knowledge Bases source attribution shows the sources behind a R A G answer. Exam tip: Model Cards document your own models, while A I Service Cards describe A W S's services.

1.title: Open Source Models, Data and Licensing
1.text: This slide goes beyond the guide. Open models let you inspect, host and adapt the model, so they are often more transparent. But open does not mean unrestricted or safe: read the license for commercial use and limits. Ask for the training data: its sources, categories and licenses. Closed models may disclose only a model card or a service card. And document your choices in a Model Card, and evaluate every model on your own task. Exam tip: check the license and the data before you adopt any model.

1.title: Trade-Offs: Safety, Transparency, Interpretability and Performance
1.text: This slide also goes beyond the guide. There are two trade-offs. Interpretability against performance: simple models are easier to explain, while complex models often perform better but are harder to explain. And safety against transparency: openness helps audits and trust, but revealing too much, such as safety rules, can help attackers. Measure both interpretability and performance, and pick the balance the risk allows. High-stakes decisions about people lean toward explainable models and human review. Exam tip: simple and explainable versus complex and accurate, so weigh both against the risk.

1.title: Human-Centered Design for Explainable AI
1.text: This slide goes beyond the guide as well. Human-centered design means designing with users, not only for them. A I decision transparency means saying when A I is used, showing sources and reasons, and stating limits. User feedback mechanisms include ratings, corrections and ways to report problems. Human oversight lets people review, challenge and escalate; Amazon A two I supports human review. And you learn from feedback to improve the system. Exam tip: tell users when A I is used, show why, and give them a way to respond.

1.title: What the Exam Asks: Transparency and Explainability
1.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Which kind of model: transparent, explainable or neither. Which tool: SageMaker Model Cards, Bedrock Model Evaluation, A I Service Cards or Clarify. Which source: open source models, data and licensing. Which trade-off: interpretability versus performance, or safety versus transparency. And which design principle: user feedback and decision transparency. Exam tip: name the need first. Is it to document, explain, evaluate or involve users?

1.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt Explains Itself
1.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and name the answer. Record a model's purpose, risk and test results for auditors: a SageMaker Model Card. Show a guest why the model refused a reward: an explainable model, with Clarify feature explanations. Evidence of quality and toxicity before launch: Bedrock Model Evaluation. Choose an open source model for hosting: check the license and training data, and evaluate it. Simple but weaker, or complex but strong: weigh interpretability against performance, and add human review. And let guests flag wrong answers: a user feedback mechanism. Pause the video if you want more time.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Transparent is how it was built, and explainable is why it answered. The tools are SageMaker Model Cards, A I Service Cards, Clarify and Bedrock Model Evaluation. For open models, check the license and the training data. The trade-offs are interpretability against performance, and safety against transparency. And human-centered design uses feedback, decision transparency and human oversight.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Which A W S tool documents a model's intended uses, risk rating, training details and evaluation results in one place? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards. They document critical details about a model for governance and reporting. Guardrails filters content, Config tracks configuration, and Macie finds sensitive data.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which statement best describes an explainable model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: it can give reasons for why it produced an output. Explainability means people can understand why a model produced an output, for example which input features mattered. It is about reasons, not size, repeatability or the source of the training data.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Select two. Which two features help users trust an A I application? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Human-centered design for explainable A I includes user feedback mechanisms and decision transparency, such as disclosing A I use and showing sources. Hiding A I use, removing reasons and blocking human review reduce trust.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Cedar and Salt must explain reward decisions to guests, and is choosing between model types. Which trade-off should the team weigh? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: simpler models are easier to interpret, but complex ones often perform better. For decisions that affect people, weigh both, measure both, and add human review.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all four answers. Question one: A. Question two: C. Question three: A and C. Question four: B. That completes Module twelve, and Domain four. Next, Module thirteen opens Domain five, with how to secure A I systems.
